research:ai.body:
Modern biology produces data faster than people can read it. A single sequencing run, proteome or interaction screen can hold millions of measurements, and the questions that matter — which gene, which protein, which interaction — are buried inside. Machine learning gives us a way to learn those patterns from known examples and apply them, consistently and at scale, to everything that is not yet characterised.

Our approach

KAABiL develops supervised models, from support vector machines to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, that learn directly from protein and nucleotide sequences. We pay as much attention to the inputs as to the models: careful benchmark datasets, feature encodings that capture composition, evolution and structure, and honest evaluation on independent data. Where uncertainty matters, we complement these with Bayesian and other unsupervised approaches.

What we build

  • Deep-learning predictors such as AtSubP-2.0, RSLpred-2.0, PRGminer, deepHPI and deepNEC, each released as a free web server.
  • Feature engineering with ProFeatX, a parallelised suite of 32 protein encodings that turns sequences into model-ready inputs.
  • Reproducible pipelines that run on the lab’s high-performance computing cluster and scale from single proteins to whole proteomes.

Questions we ask

  • Can a model trained on well-studied species annotate proteins in crops and pathogens that have little experimental data?
  • Which sequence features carry the signal, and what do they tell us about the biology?
  • How do we make predictions trustworthy and easy to use for bench scientists?

The lab has applied machine learning to biology since its first work on disease forecasting in 2006, and every tool listed on this page is free for academic research.

research:hpi.body:
Every infectious disease is a conversation between two genomes. Pathogen proteins bind host proteins to enter cells, suppress immunity and take over metabolism; host proteins recognise and resist them. Mapping these protein–protein interactions reveals how disease works and points to targets for resistant crops, drugs and vaccines. Experimental screens cover only a small fraction of possible pairs, so computational prediction is essential.

Our approach

We predict host–pathogen interactomes at genome scale by combining interolog and domain-based inference with sequence-based machine learning and deep learning. Predicted networks are filtered, annotated with function, localisation and pathway information, and analysed with systems-biology methods to find the hubs and bottlenecks that matter most.

Systems we study

  • Crop diseases: wheat stem rust (TRustDB), stripe rust (StripeNET), common bunt (WeCoNET) and Karnal bunt (TritiKBdb); alfalfa bacterial stem blight (alfaNET); citrus greening (GreeningDB); and the Arabidopsis–Pseudomonas model (AP-iNET).
  • Human viruses: SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses (HuCoPIA, HuCoVarIA, Malivhu) and monkeypox (HuPoxNET).
  • General platforms: PredHPI, deepHPI and HPIpy let researchers predict and visualise interactions for their own host–pathogen pairs.

Why it matters

Interaction atlases turn a pathogen genome into a list of testable hypotheses: which host proteins are targeted, which pathways are disrupted, and which interactions could be blocked. Our databases are designed to help researchers prioritise candidate resistance genes in crops and potential drug targets in human disease.

research:pfp.body:
Sequencing a genome is now routine; knowing what its proteins do is not. For most crops and pathogens the majority of proteins have never been studied experimentally. Where a protein works inside the cell — nucleus, chloroplast, mitochondrion, membrane — and what family it belongs to are two of the most informative clues to its function.

Our approach

We build predictors that annotate entire proteomes from sequence alone. Our models learn from curated, experimentally verified examples and combine amino-acid composition, evolutionary profiles and learned sequence features, increasingly through deep neural networks. Several predictors handle proteins that live in more than one compartment, which reflects real cell biology better than single-label methods.

What we build

  • Subcellular localisation: AtSubP-2.0 for Arabidopsis, RSLpred-2.0 for rice, Plant-mSubP for plants in general, LegumeLoc for legumes and PLpred for plastid types.
  • Gene families with practical value: PRGminer finds plant resistance genes; LacSubPred and LigPred classify laccases and lignin-related proteins relevant to bioenergy.
  • Features for any model: ProFeatX extracts protein descriptors in parallel for researchers building their own classifiers.

This line of work began with RSLpred (2009) and the Arabidopsis localisation work published in Plant Physiology (2010), and continues with deep-learning versions released in 2025.

research:metagenomics.body:
A gram of agricultural soil holds billions of microbes, most of which have never been grown in a laboratory. Their enzymes drive the nitrogen cycle that determines how much fertiliser a crop can actually use — and how much is lost to the environment. Metagenomics reads the DNA of the whole community at once, but most of the genes it recovers have no known function.

Our approach

We develop alignment-free, deep-learning methods that recognise enzyme families directly from sequence, so that genes can be identified even when they share little similarity with anything in reference databases. Applied to soil metagenomes, these models recover candidate genes for each step of the nitrogen biochemical network and help connect microbial communities to crop performance.

What we build

  • deepNEC and deepNEC-2.0 identify and classify nitrogen-cycle enzymes in genomic and metagenomic data.
  • MINpred, a further predictor in the lab’s metagenomics toolset.
  • Related work on plant–microbe symbiosis studies the small secreted proteins that mediate arbuscular mycorrhizal partnerships.

Why it matters

Better maps of soil microbial function support more efficient fertiliser use, healthier soils and crop varieties that cooperate with their microbial partners.

research:pa.body:
Precision agriculture uses data, sensors and models to make farm decisions plot by plot instead of field by field: when to spray, where to weed, which variety to plant. The lab’s interest here goes back to its earliest work, which used machine learning to forecast rice blast — one of the most destructive crop diseases — from weather data.

Our approach

We combine predictive modelling with field and genetic data. Disease-forecasting models give growers advance warning so that treatments can be timed rather than applied by calendar. Student projects apply computer vision and AI to recognise weeds, the basis for robotic systems that remove weeds selectively and reduce herbicide use. Genome-wide marker databases support breeders selecting resilient varieties.

What we build

  • RBPred, a rice blast prediction server built on the lab’s forecasting research.
  • Simple sequence repeat (SSR) marker databases for breeding: citSATdb (citrus), legumeSSRdb (legumes) and ranchSATdb (livestock).
  • AI-based weed recognition, developed by undergraduate researchers — see the story about this project.

research:ngs.body:
Next-generation sequencing measures genomes, transcriptomes, small RNAs and DNA methylation at a scale that was unimaginable twenty years ago. The challenge has moved from producing data to analysing it correctly: aligning billions of reads, calling variants, quantifying expression and turning the results into biological insight.

Our approach

We design and run end-to-end analysis pipelines on the lab’s high-performance computing cluster and package them so that others can reproduce them. Our analyses combine RNA-seq, miRNA-seq, whole-genome sequencing and variant data with network and pathway methods to explain how plants and animals respond to their environment.

What we study

  • Crop stress: transcriptomes, miRNomes and regulatory networks of rice under reproductive-stage drought, barley under heat and drought, and alfalfa under salt stress.
  • Pathogen genomes: whole-genome sequencing and comparative analysis, for example of the oomycete root pathogen Pythium brassicum.
  • Methods and software: pySeqRNA, a Python package for RNA-seq analysis, contributions to the NGSEP3 variant caller, and genome-wide marker databases.

This work frequently connects with our other areas: expression data feed interaction networks, and newly sequenced genomes are annotated with our protein function predictors.

tools:stripenet.summary: Protein–protein interactions between wheat and stripe rust strains, to uncover disease mechanisms and support durable resistance.

tools:predhpi.summary: Web platform to detect and visualise host–pathogen interactions with sequence-based methods.

tools:apinet.summary: Predicted host–pathogen protein interactions in the Arabidopsis–Pseudomonas syringae model system.

tools:plantmSubp.summary: Single- and multi-target protein subcellular localisation for plants using integrated machine learning.

tools:atSubP.summary: Subcellular localisation of Arabidopsis proteins combining machine learning and homology.

tools:rslPredP.summary: Subcellular localisation of rice proteins from compositional and evolutionary information.

tools:plPred.summary: Prediction of plastid-type proteins from sequence features using machine learning.

tools:greeningDB.summary: Host–pathogen interactions and annotation of the bacteria that cause citrus greening (huanglongbing).

tools:citSATdb.summary: Genome-wide SSR marker database of citrus species for germplasm characterisation and breeding.

tools:legumeSSRdb.summary: Microsatellite (SSR) marker database of legumes for germplasm characterisation and crop improvement.

tools:lacSubPred.summary: Predicts subtypes of laccases, lignin-metabolism enzymes important for biofuels and industry.

tools:ligPred.summary: Discovers novel lignin-related proteins for bioenergy research.

tools:rbPred.summary: Rice blast prediction server built on machine-learning disease forecasting.

tools:necMiner.summary: Alignment-free deep learning for nitrogen-cycle enzyme identification and classification.

tools:deepHPI.summary: Deep-learning prediction and visualisation of host–pathogen protein–protein interactions for plant, human and animal pathogens.

tools:huco.summary: Atlas of about 100,000 interactions between human proteins and SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV and MERS.

tools:ranchSAT.summary: Genome-wide SSR marker database of livestock species for germplasm characterisation.

tools:alfaNet.summary: Alfalfa–bacterial stem blight protein interactions revealing molecular features of the pathogen.

tools:weconet.summary: Host–pathogen interactome of wheat and common bunt, revealing key molecular networks.

tools:malivhu.summary: Filters SARS and MERS virus proteins and predicts their interactions with human proteins.

tools:trustdb.summary: Wheat–stem rust protein interactions with functional annotation of Puccinia proteins.

tools:tritikbdb.summary: Interaction networks and functional annotation for the wheat–Karnal bunt pathosystem.

tools:HuCoVarIA.summary: Resource on SARS-CoV-2 variants and their interactions with human proteins.

tools:ProFeatX.summary: Parallelised extraction of 32 protein feature encodings for machine learning.

tools:pySeqRNA.summary: Python package for end-to-end RNA-seq data analysis.

tools:AtSubP2.summary: Deep-learning (CNN + RNN) subcellular localisation of the Arabidopsis proteome.

tools:RSLpred2.summary: Deep-learning subcellular localisation of the rice proteome.

tools:deepNEC2.summary: Updated deep-learning models for nitrogen-cycle enzyme prediction.

tools:PRGminer.summary: Deep learning to identify and classify plant resistance (R) genes.

tools:HuPoxNET.summary: Atlas of the human–monkeypox virus interactome for functional insights.

tools:HPIpy.summary: Python toolkit to predict host–pathogen protein interactions.

when.summary: Kaundal Artificial Intelligence & Advanced Bioinformatics Laboratory at Utah State University: Bridging biology, computation, and engineering from information to inference.
when.body:
Biology. Data. Discovery.

The Kaundal Artificial Intelligence & Advanced Bioinformatics Laboratory (KAABiL) is an interdisciplinary research group based in the Department of Plants, Soils and Climate and the Center for Integrated BioSystems at Utah State University, directed by Dr. Rakesh Kaundal.

Biological data is accumulating exponentially, far outpacing conventional analytical capacity. Our research program addresses this fundamental bottleneck under the paradigm of “Information to Inference”—harnessing statistical pattern recognition, artificial intelligence (AI), and deep learning architectures to transform high-dimensional multi-omics datasets into biological discovery, crop resilience, and therapeutic insights.

Core Research Thrusts

AI & Machine Learning in Biology

Developing predictive algorithms, deep neural networks, and supervised/unsupervised models for protein subcellular localization, resistance gene discovery, and functional genomic annotation.

Host-Pathogen Interactions

Modeling cross-kingdom inter- and intra-species interaction networks to decode the molecular mechanisms of virulence, pathogen evolution, and plant/animal immune defense.

Metagenomics & Crop Improvement

Engineering bioinformatics solutions for agri-microbiomes and soil metagenomes, identifying novel biocatalytic enzymes and optimizing the nitrogen cycle for sustainable agriculture.

Advanced NGS Big Data Analytics

Analyzing petabytes of high-throughput sequencing data across transcriptomics (RNA-seq, miRNA-seq), epigenomics (Methyl-seq), genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS), and de novo genome assembly.

“We bring together biology, computer science, mathematics, and engineering to solve high-impact challenges in computational biology and train the next generation of data scientists.”

— Dr. Rakesh Kaundal, Director of Bioinformatics Facility & Associate Professor

Open-Access Infrastructure & Global Tools

A central commitment of KAABiL is delivering high-impact, reproducible software, web servers, and databases freely accessible to researchers worldwide. Our laboratory maintains over 35 public bioinformatics resources hosted on Utah State University infrastructure, including the USU BioinfoCore, HPC cluster pipelines, and specialized diagnostic portals.

set.summary: An interdisciplinary bioinformatics research group at Utah State University, led by Dr. Rakesh Kaundal.
set.body:
The Kaundal Artificial Intelligence & Advanced Bioinformatics Lab (KAABiL) is led by Dr. Rakesh Kaundal, Associate Professor of Bioinformatics in the Department of Plants, Soils and Climate and Director of the Bioinformatics Facility at the Center for Integrated BioSystems, Utah State University.

We bring together biology, computer science, engineering and related disciplines to train the next generation of data scientists.

What we work on

The group applies statistical pattern recognition, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to systems biology, metagenomics, regulatory mechanisms of gene expression, genome-wide host–pathogen interaction networks and genome annotation for functional studies.

We develop computational tools and algorithms for pathogen detection and discrimination, the identification of species-specific signatures, and AI-based prediction of biochemical pathways and structure–function relationships.

Collaboration

A key strength of the program is collaboration: making sense of complex -omics data from next-generation sequencing experiments, such as transcriptomics (RNA-seq), miRNA-seq, methylation patterns (Methyl-seq), genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) and the assembly of novel genomes.

when.title: Research and lab overview
when.body:
Welcome to the Kaundal Artificial Intelligence & Advanced Bioinformatics Lab (KAABiL). We bring together biology, computer science, and engineering to train the next generation of data scientists and solve complex biological problems.

Our Mission

Modern biology produces data faster than we can interpret it. From high-throughput sequencing to complex agricultural microbiomes, the questions that matter are hidden within massive datasets. At KAABiL, our mission is to develop cutting-edge computational tools, databases, and machine learning models to bridge this gap. We focus on computational mining and modeling of complex multi-dimensional OMICS datasets using supervised and unsupervised learning techniques.

Research Themes

Our research focuses on several core areas that intersect computer science and biology:

  • Artificial Intelligence: Developing deep learning algorithms to predict protein and nucleotide functions directly from sequence data.
  • Host-Pathogen Interactions: Modeling the evolutionary arms race between plants/animals and their pathogens to identify novel therapeutic targets.
  • Metagenomics & Soil Health: Annotating agricultural microbiomes to discover novel enzymes involved in the nitrogen cycle.
  • Precision Agriculture: Applying AI and machine learning to field data, including robotic weed recognition and genome-wide marker databases for crop resilience.
  • Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS): Creating robust pipelines for RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and whole-genome analysis.

For more detailed information on specific projects, please visit our main Research page to explore our published databases, tools, and ongoing studies.

Education & Training

We are deeply committed to training. To date, Dr. Kaundal has trained numerous graduate and undergraduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and full-time bioinformatics staff. We believe that empowering researchers with cross-disciplinary skills is the key to solving tomorrow's challenges.

set.title: Lab overview
set.summary: How the lab works: the Bioinformatics Facility, open tools, collaborative sequencing analysis and training.
set.body:
Bioinformatics Facility

Dr. Kaundal directs the Bioinformatics Facility at the Center for Integrated BioSystems (CIB), Utah State University. One of the program’s objectives is to establish high-end biocomputing infrastructure, including a high-performance computing cluster, and novel AI algorithms to advance big-data research.

Open tools and databases

The lab develops cost-effective prediction tools and databases and publishes them as customized, searchable web portals. They are listed on Tools & databases.

Collaborative sequencing analysis

Collaborative projects range from routine bioinformatics data mining to complex NGS projects such as RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, SNP-seq, Methyl-seq, miRNA-seq, GBS and genome assembly. To discuss a project, contact the lab.

Training

Lab members range from graduate students to undergraduates and come from a wide variety of disciplines. Dr. Kaundal has trained more than 10 graduate students, 10 undergraduate students, a postdoctoral fellow and 3 full-time bioinformatics staff members in his research program.

Meet the current team on People, or see Opportunities to join.

when.title: Connect with KAABiL
when.body:
If you would like to join us, we are always looking for independently-funded research fellows or extended visitors. Please use the form below to explore our options. Summer student positions are also available for up to a 3 - 4 month period.

A number of research projects are available within the general areas of bioinformatics, computational systems biology, biological bigdata mining, comparative genomics, and functional genomics in KAABiL lab. Postdoctoral researchers, research higher degree (PhD and Masters), honours and undergraduate students are welcome to join our group.

Masters and Honors

Students are required to have a good understanding of biomolecular sciences and computer programming as well as experience in supervised learning and unsupervised learning (Bayesian-based). Students will need to demonstrate adaptability to the multidisciplinary nature of our projects. Masters and honors students are encouraged to contact Dr. Kaundal to express interest. Both degree options in either the Department of Computer Science or Department of Plants, Soils & Climate are available.

PhD

PhD opportunities with government and university-funded scholarships are available each year to domestic and international students. Knowledge or experience with scripting languages (Perl, Python) and statistical/mathematical toolkits (R, Matlab) with some kind of programming experience in C, C++, or Java is preferable. Both degree options in either the Department of Computer Science or Department of Plants, Soils & Climate are available.

Key Criteria

Domestic students – Students should have a strong academic track record (including research and write-up) with first class honours. The student’s research and academic background might be in one or more of biological sciences (plant/animal), mathematics, statistics, computer science, data analytics, biological engineering and related life science disciplines.

International students – International students are expected to have masters and honours degrees with a strong academic and research background in a relevant field. An overall IELTS score of 6.0+ with a minimum score of 5 in each band is preferable. This can be subtituted with a TOEFL score of 79+. For more details on eligibility, please visit the USU graduate school website.

Postdoctoral Research Fellow

A postdoctoral research fellow with strong research and publication records in the area of bioinformatics and computational biology is encouraged to directly contact Dr. Kaundal to express interest.

Key Criteria

A PhD in one or more biological sciences (plant/animal), mathematics, statistics, computer science, data analytics, biological engineering, or any related discipline in life sciences is required, along with strong evidence of prior productivity and high-impact publications.

set.title: Joining the lab
set.summary: Who can join, and eligibility for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Shown on the Opportunities page.
set.body:
We are always looking for independently funded research fellows and extended visitors. Summer student positions are also available for up to 3–4 months.

Research projects are available in bioinformatics, computational systems biology, biological big-data mining, comparative genomics and functional genomics. Postdoctoral researchers, research higher-degree students (PhD and Master’s), honours and undergraduate students are welcome to join the group.

Master’s and honours students

Students need a good understanding of biomolecular sciences and computer programming, and experience in supervised and unsupervised (Bayesian-based) learning, and should be ready for the multidisciplinary nature of our projects. Degree options are available in the Department of Computer Science or the Department of Plants, Soils & Climate.

PhD students

PhD opportunities with government and university-funded scholarships are available each year to domestic and international students. Experience with scripting languages (Perl, Python) and statistical or mathematical toolkits (R, Matlab), and some programming in C, C++ or Java, is preferred. Degree options are available in either department.

Key criteria

  • Domestic students: a strong academic track record (including research and write-up) with first-class honours, and a background in one or more of the biological sciences (plant/animal), mathematics, statistics, computer science, data analytics, biological engineering or related life-science disciplines.
  • International students: a master’s or honours degree with a strong academic and research background in a relevant field. An overall IELTS score of 6.0+ (minimum 5 in each band) is preferred; a TOEFL score of 79+ can be substituted. Eligibility details are on the USU School of Graduate Studies website.

Postdoctoral research fellows

Researchers with strong research and publication records in bioinformatics and computational biology are encouraged to contact Dr. Kaundal directly.

Key criteria

A PhD in one or more of the biological sciences (plant/animal), mathematics, statistics, computer science, data analytics, biological engineering or a related life-science discipline, with strong evidence of prior productivity and high-impact publications.
